title: Title and the 'terrible sonnets'
short: One of the 'terrible' or 'dark' sonnets written in Dublin in 1885. The title was supplied by Bridges from the first line.
body: Hopkins left the poem untitled. Robert Bridges named it from its first line when he published it in 1918. It belongs to the group of sonnets of desolation written in 1885, while Hopkins was Professor of Greek at University College Dublin, isolated, overworked and depressed. On 17 May 1885 he wrote to Bridges that he had after long silence written two sonnets, and that if anything was ever written in blood one of them was. He does not name them, and 'Carrion Comfort' is one of the candidates proposed. 'Carrion comfort' is the comfort of feeding on dead flesh. Despair is personified as a corpse the speaker is tempted to feast on, a 'comfort' that is really death. In Catholic theology despair is a sin against hope.

sources.cite: Robert Bridges (ed.), Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins (Humphrey Milford, 1918), poem and notes
C. C. Abbott (ed.), The Letters of Gerard Manley Hopkins to Robert Bridges (Oxford UP, 1935), letter of 17 May 1885
Norman H. MacKenzie (ed.), The Poetical Works of Gerard Manley Hopkins (Clarendon Press, 1990), notes on 'Carrion Comfort'

title: Form: the long-lined sonnet
short: A Petrarchan sonnet (abbaabba cdcdcd) in very long lines of sprung rhythm, each with six or more stresses and outriding syllables.
body: The poem keeps the Italian sonnet's rhyme scheme and octave–sestet turn. But its lines are stretched to six or more stresses, with extra slack syllables and spill-over (shown in the archive by indented continuations such as 'me? scan'). Hopkins's stress marks (ór, chéer, fóot tród) tell the reader where to put the weight. The jostling, broken syntax of repetitions, questions and parentheses enacts the inner struggle it describes. The volta comes at line 9: 'Why? That my chaff might fly'.

sources.cite: Norman H. MacKenzie (ed.), The Poetical Works of Gerard Manley Hopkins (Clarendon Press, 1990), notes on 'Carrion Comfort'

title: Last strands of man
short: The self is a frayed rope. The speaker refuses to untwist its last strands, however 'slack' they may be.
body: The image is of a rope or cord whose strands hold a man together. Despair would untwist them and leave nothing. The parenthesis '(slack they may be)' admits weakness but holds on. The verb 'untwist' gives the refusal a physical, hand-to-hand quality, preparing for the wrestling of the close. The sequence of negatives at the start ('NOT, I'll not ... Not untwist ... not choose not to be') makes refusal itself an act of resistance.

anchor: I can no more. I can
title: I can no more. I can
short: The speaker refuses to cry 'I can no more', and answers at once, 'I can', a minimal assertion of will.
body: 'I can no more' is the cry of the exhausted. Hopkins puts it on the speaker's lips only to reverse it in two words: 'I can'. Line 4 then specifies how little can be done: 'Can something, hope, wish day come, not choose not to be'. The double negative of 'not choose not to be' is a refusal of suicide, which recalls Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be' (3.1). The speaker's resistance amounts only to not choosing death, but the poem treats that as a real victory.

title: O thou terrible
short: The 'terrible' one who tramples the speaker is God, felt as a violent antagonist. Some readers take it as Despair, or as both.
body: With 'But ah, but O thou terrible' the address changes. Most critics identify the terrible one as God, whose overwhelming power the speaker experiences as assault, much as in Job. The sestet confirms this when the opponent is named 'my God'. A few readers hear Despair still being addressed in the octave, which would make the poem's identification of the enemy part of its drama. Since the speaker is unsure whether his tormentor is a demon or the God who chastens, he cannot tell despair from purgation.

title: rude (as verb)
short: 'Rude' is used as a verb: to treat roughly or to rock violently. Its syntax is completed in the next line by 'Thy wring-world right foot rock'.
body: The syntax is contorted: 'why wouldst thou rude on me / Thy wring-world right foot rock?' The usual reading is 'why would you roughly rock your world-wringing right foot on me?'. 'Rude' is an adjective made into a verb or adverb, meaning to act rudely, roughly. The heavy alliteration (r, w) and clustered stresses make the line feel like crushing weight. Editors disagree about the exact grammar, and Hopkins's compressions often allow more than one construction.

title: Wring-world right foot
short: God's right foot can 'wring' the whole world. It is rocked onto the prostrate speaker like a conqueror's foot on the vanquished.
body: 'Wring-world' is a compound epithet: the foot that wrings, twists or crushes the world. It recalls biblical images of enemies made a footstool and the victor's foot on the neck of the defeated (Joshua 10:24; Psalm 110:1). One student essay on the Victorian Web notes that the foot is likened to a rock. The 'right' foot and 'right' hand carry biblical associations of divine power.

title: Lionlimb
short: God as lion recalls Job's complaint 'Thou huntest me as a fierce lion' (Job 10:16).
body: Job laments that God hunts him 'as a fierce lion' (Job 10:16), and the prophets compare God to a lion tearing his people (Hosea 13:7–8). Hopkins's compound 'lionlimb' makes the divine attacker a beast whose heavy paw is laid on the speaker. The following questions continue the predatory image: God scans him 'With darksome devouring eyes' and looks at his 'bruisèd bones' (an echo of the Psalmist's 'bones which thou hast broken', Psalm 51:8). The poem's whole octave is a Joblike complaint against God's apparent cruelty.

title: Fan: the winnowing fan
short: 'Fan' means to winnow, as with the winnowing fan that separates grain from chaff. It is explained in the sestet's 'chaff' and 'grain'.
body: At first 'fan, / O in turns of tempest, me heaped there' sounds like blowing on a heap of something. The next line explains it. A fan is the winnowing fan or basket used to toss threshed grain into the wind so the light chaff blows away. John the Baptist says of Christ, 'Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff' (Matthew 3:12). The speaker lies 'heaped' like grain on a threshing-floor, battered by a tempest of winnowing.

title: Chaff and grain
short: The volta answers 'Why?': the suffering was purgation, so that the worthless chaff might be blown away and the pure grain remain.
body: The sestet begins with the answer to the octave's questions. The suffering has a purpose: 'That my chaff might fly; my grain lie, sheer and clear'. 'Sheer' here means pure, unmixed. The image of winnowing, prepared by 'fan', turns the apparent cruelty into purification, in line with traditional Christian accounts of affliction as God's discipline (Hebrews 12:6). The tone changes from complaint to understanding, though the closing lines show the understanding to be hard-won and unsettled.

title: Kissed the rod
short: To 'kiss the rod' is to accept punishment submissively, a proverbial phrase. The parenthesis '(seems)' shows the speaker is unsure he has really done so.
body: The proverbial expression 'to kiss the rod' meant to accept chastisement meekly, as a child kisses the rod it is beaten with. It appears, for example, in Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona (1.2). Hopkins's parenthetical '(seems)' makes the submission uncertain, as though he cannot be sure that he has truly accepted God's will. 'Toil' and 'coil' (turmoil, as in Hamlet's 'mortal coil') rhyme internally to describe the struggle.

sources.cite: Shakespeare, The Two Gentlemen of Verona 1.2 (Folger Shakespeare)

title: Hand rather
short: He corrects himself. It was not the rod he kissed but the hand that wielded it, so punishment is turned into personal relation with God.
body: 'Hand rather' corrects the previous phrase. Kissing the hand instead of the rod shifts the stress from the instrument of punishment to the person who punishes, and the gesture becomes one of homage or love, like kissing a lord's or a priest's hand. With that the speaker's heart is renewed. It 'lapped strength, stole joy, would laugh, chéer', a cascade of verbs that recovers vitality. 'Lapped' means drank, like an animal lapping water.

title: lapped strength, stole joy
short: The heart drank in strength as an animal laps water and 'stole' joy, as if it were not quite entitled to it.
body: 'Lapped' means drank by lapping, with an animal eagerness. Some readers recall Gideon's soldiers who 'lapped' water from their hands and were chosen for battle (Judges 7:5–7), though the echo is uncertain. 'Stole joy' suggests a happiness taken almost guiltily in the midst of suffering. The stress mark on 'chéer' prepares for the question in l. 12, 'Cheer whom though?', which turns the word over and examines it.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Judges 7:5

title: Cheer whom though?
short: Whom should he cheer, the 'hero' God who flung him down, or himself who fought? The poem answers 'each one'.
body: The question unsettles the moment of joy. Is the heart to applaud 'the hero whose heaven-handling flung me' (God, whose heavenly strength threw him down, 'fóot tród / Me') or 'me that fought him'? The answer, 'is it each one?', gives credit to both sides. This is the paradox of a struggle in which being defeated by God is also victory. Critics compare the Holy Sonnets of Donne, where the speaker asks God to batter and overthrow him. 'Heaven-handling' is a compound coinage for divine grip and dexterity.

sources.cite: Paul L. Mariani, A Commentary on the Complete Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins (Cornell UP, 1970), on 'Carrion Comfort'

title: Wrestling with my God
short: Like Jacob wrestling with God at night (Genesis 32), the speaker finds his opponent was God; '(my God!) my God' is both oath and recognition.
body: In Genesis 32:24–30 Jacob wrestles all night with a mysterious man who turns out to be God ('I have seen God face to face'). He is lamed but blessed. Hopkins's ending recalls this. 'That night, that year / Of now done darkness' places the struggle in the past ('now done'), but 'I wretch' keeps its misery present. The last words are carefully punctuated. The first '(my God!)' is an exclamation of horror, the second 'my God' is the identification of the opponent, God, who is still 'my' God. The pairing is widely seen as the poem's central paradox: the enemy is the beloved Lord.
